Se redécouvrir pour passer à l’action :: Rediscovering Yourself to Take Action: An Interview with Daphne-Anne Olepika Takpanie Kiguktak
L’an dernier, j’ai perdu mon amie Kelly: “Last year, I lost my friend Kelly Fraser. She was going through a lot of lateral violence. It awakened a need in me.”
Pour comprendre et savoir où on va, il f: To understand and know where we’re going, we have to know where we come from. That is the message Daphne-Anne Olepika Takpanie Kiguktak, founder of YIWA-Young Indigenous Women Action/Jeunes Femmes Autochtones En Action, shares with us as she opens up about her journey.
On parle de ses inspirations, de la soli: We talk about her inspirations, solidarity among Indigenous women, healing and, above all, rediscovering oneself.
<strong>D’où vient ton besoin de te réun: Where does your need to come together with Indigenous women come from?
L’an dernier, j’ai perdu mon amie Kelly: Last year, I lost my friend Kelly Fraser. She was going through a lot of lateral violence. It awakened a need in me. A deep need, one that goes back several years, for us to come together as Indigenous women and do things together, to create spaces for ourselves. Beautiful things happen when we see each other, gather, and raise our voices.
J’ai réalisé que le chemin que je devais: I realized that the path I had to follow to reach that goal was to create a non-profit organization. It has been registered since last summer: it’s called Young Indigenous Women Action/Jeunes Femmes Autochtones En Action.
Il vise à mettre en œuvre des programmes: It aims to implement land-based healing programs for young Indigenous women. The goal is to give them tools for their future, their people and their environment. I had a project, but I didn’t have the tools to carry it out. So I decided to go to university.
Je ne savais même pas que c’était possib: I didn’t even know it was possible for me. I didn’t go to CEGEP. I finished high school very late, a few years ago, at 25. I did a program called ACCÈS-FEP, which exists for people who want to pursue university studies and have an atypical background. I’m now in my third university semester.
En ce moment, j’étudie à temps plein à l: Right now, I’m studying full time at Université de Montréal, where I’m completing a certificate in philanthropic management. I’m learning everything related to philanthropy: managing a non-profit, development strategy, frameworks and standards, and more.
<strong>Quelle est ta connexion avec ta: What is your connection to your culture and your identity?
Il y a quelques années, je vivais du str: A few years ago, I was dealing with stress related to lateral violence. I would get judgments like, “You’re not Indigenous, because of this or that.” Then that’s when I felt a desperate need to reconnect with my land, with my family.
Ma mère biologique, parmi tant d’autres,: My birth mother, like so many others, suffered through residential schools, and it caused trauma. Because of that, she wasn’t able to take care of me. So she entrusted me to someone else in her life, a Québécoise woman who took care of me. Both of my mothers were there to welcome me into this life.
J’ai grandi loin de mon territoire, de l: I grew up far from my land and my culture, and it was super important to me to find them again as soon as possible. I felt really lost, caught between two worlds.
Ç’a créé un vide à l’intérieur de moi. J: It created a void inside me. At one point I told myself enough was enough, that I had to go back to my land and meet my family.
Du jour au lendemain, j’ai mis mes affai: Overnight, I put my things in a box, took my backpack and left for the North. That’s where a great adventure began. I went to meet my birth family for the first time, in Grise Fiord, Nunavut.
ᐊᐅᔪᐃᑦᑐᖅ, Ausuittuq – c’est le nom de la: ᐊᐅᔪᐃᑦᑐᖅ, Ausuittuq – that’s the name of the community in Inuktitut. It means “the place where the ice never melts.” There are fewer than 150 residents. It was quite an experience!
Grise Giord, Ausuittuq, à l’aube. Photo:: Grise Fiord, Ausuittuq, at dawn. Photo: Daphne-Anne Olepika Takpanie Kiguktak
Quand je suis dans le Sud, le Nord me ma: When I’m in the South, I miss the North. When I’m in the North, I miss the South too. The two places represent something so different and so important. I’ll feel this pull for the rest of my life. At the same time, it’s something very beautiful that makes me who I am. As for my name, it was a personal debate for a long time. The woman who raised me called me Daphne-Anne, but my birth mother named me Olepika.
J’ai grandi en portant ce premier prénom: I grew up with that first name. Later, as an adult, while I was discovering certain things about the story of my life, I started asking people to call me Olepika. In my personal history, there was a separation between Daphne-Anne and Olepika. Today, as I approach thirty, I realize that I have enormous respect for both of my names. In fact, it’s not just my name, it’s the story of my life.
<strong>Quels sont les éléments qui te t: What matters most to you, and what do you want to bring into your project?
Il y a toujours un lien avec le territoi: There’s always a connection to the land in everything I do. Without the land, without our environment, we wouldn’t get anywhere. We mustn’t forget that, and we have to take care of our planet. All of YIWA’s programs will have a connection to the land. To strengthen that connection, I want to develop a sailboat program.
Je vois un lien clair entre la voile et: I see a clear link between sailing and Indigenous communities. On a sailboat, we all have different strengths and different roles to make the boat run. It’s together that we manage to move forward. That’s the link: with the different communities, together, with our different strengths, we will succeed in changing things for our peoples and our environment.
<strong>Qu’est-ce qui t’inspire à aller: What inspires you to keep moving forward?
Cela fait plusieurs années que je suis i: I’ve been involved in the environmental field, in protecting the land, for several years. I got involved in different groups, where I was often the only Indigenous woman. I wondered where they were, and why I was the only one. I wanted to see a beautiful generation of Indigenous women getting involved.
C’est de là que m’est venue l’idée de cr: That’s where the idea of creating YIWA came from, to build a creative space for Indigenous women so that we can build something solid together for our future. The idea also came to me from seeing the absence of Indigenous women in the media. A few years ago, it was shocking to see how few there were.
Tranquillement, les gens commencent à s’: Slowly, people are starting to take an interest in Indigenous peoples; we’re being given more space. With colonization, the place of Indigenous women has changed so much. We’re so erased. We disappear, we’re murdered in this country, and it’s so alarming. It’s truly urgent that we take back our place. That people also realize how sacred women are. We have to rediscover that respect for women.
